about: The open weights for the five parcel pillars. Every indicator, source, normalization rule, weight and gate lives here; the build script, the scorer, the methodology page and the chatbot all read this file. Change a weight here (or pass an override file to score-parcels.ts) and every score changes. Weights are value judgments, not data.
scale: Every indicator, sub-score and pillar is 0–100, where 100 means this is a good place to build new housing and 0 means a poor one.
reference: Area indicators are percentile-ranked across all Allegheny County units in their source file (block groups, tracts or ZIPs); parcel indicators use fixed thresholds.

missing.rule: exclude and renormalize the remaining weights

overall.rationale: Weighted geometric mean limits how much a strong pillar can offset a weak one (UN HDI, 2010 switch; OECD/JRC Handbook 2008). Scores are floored at 1 so a zero doesn't zero the product. Arithmetic is available as a toggle.

hazard_multiplier.rationale: A few Site gates are deal-killers, not just a low Site score: most of the lot in the floodway, a sliver lot, or mapped mines under anything larger than a house. Capping only the Site pillar let the other four pillars average them away (a fully undermined lot moved the overall about 2%). Those gates carry an `overall` factor that multiplies the overall score, like zoning and availability; the lowest fired factor applies. Hackathon SMEs (2026-09-27) called undermining and environmental conditions up-front deal killers. Undermining gets a mild factor (×0.9) because about 30% of City parcels (43,001 of 142,365) are over mapped mines and the layer gives no depth of cover: it means a mine investigation, not a ban. The factors are value judgments.

missing_pillar.rationale: A pillar without enough data counts as that pillar's City 25th-percentile score (the per-pillar `impute` value, from the 2026-09-26 build; Site re-taken 2026-09-27 after the undermined gate started capping) and is flagged: conservative, so missing data is never rewarded (round-2 review). 50 is the fallback if a pillar has no `impute`.

pillars.label: Demand
pillars.description: Is there demand for new homes here? Household and job growth, low vacancy, an active sales market, rising rents and recent construction score high.
pillars.direction_note: Value judgment: Demand measures market strength (sales activity, low vacancy, new construction), so it correlates strongly (0.77) with the Reinvestment Fund market type that is otherwise kept at weight 0. At full weight it pulls the overall toward strong markets; Housing Need pulls toward high-need places. Lower Demand's weight to favor need.

pillars.label: Site Feasibility
pillars.description: Can this lot physically take new housing? Flooding, steep slopes, landslides, undermining and known lead service lines score low. Zoning legality is applied per housing type, not averaged in.

gates.flag: Half or more of the lot is in the FEMA regulatory floodway
Part of the lot is in the FEMA regulatory floodway
Half or more of the lot is in the 100-year floodplain (City floodplain overlay applies)
Half or more of the lot is 25%+ slope (steep-slope overlay: Planning Commission hearing, §906.08)
Half or more of the lot is landslide-prone (geotechnical study required)
Over mapped mines: anything larger than a single house is prohibited until a mine investigation clears it (§906.05)
Known lead or galvanized service line on this address

pillars.label: Affordability
pillars.description: How much unmet need for homes people can afford is here, measured by households: low-income renters who are cost-burdened and the share of renters with extremely low incomes. Displacement pressure is shown alongside as a flag, not scored.

subscores.label: Housing need
subscores.description: Unmet need among households: cost-burdened low-income renters and the share of renters at or below 30% of area median income. 100 = greatest need.

subscores.label: Displacement pressure (shown, not scored)
subscores.description: Sale-price growth relative to incomes (Reinvestment Fund DRR), recent price growth and 5-year rent growth. 100 = little pressure. Weight 0 by default; raise it in the config to score it.

pillars.direction_note: Value judgment: greater need raises the score. Displacement pressure is shown, not scored: research finds new supply tends to relieve nearby rents and displacement (Asquith, Mast & Reed 2023; Pennington 2021), and the right response to pressure is usually income-restricted homes and tenant protections, not avoiding the area. Round-1 review found that scoring price growth pushed down the poorest, mostly Black neighborhoods.

gates.flag: Sale prices outpaced local incomes by 2019/20 (Reinvestment Fund DRR, top 10% of the county): income-restricted homes and tenant protections matter most here
Strong recent home-price growth (2020–21 to 2024–25): income-restricted homes and tenant protections matter most here
Over 30% of residents are college students: income-based need measures are left out here because student households read as low-income

pillars.label: Access to Opportunity
pillars.description: Would new residents reach daily needs? Walking distance to groceries, health care, schools and services, transit service, and jobs reachable by transit.

pillars.label: Climate & Environment
pillars.description: Would homes here be low-carbon and healthy? Two sub-scores that often pull in opposite directions: carbon (dense, walkable places mean less driving) and local environment (air, heat, tree canopy). Kept separate so the trade-off stays visible.

subscores.label: Carbon (location efficiency)
subscores.description: Transportation emissions a household here would likely produce. Building-form carbon depends on the housing type and is added when types are compared.

subscores.label: Local environment
subscores.description: Air pollution, industrial emissions, surface heat and tree canopy where residents would live.

indicators.label: Household change, 2020 Census to ACS 2020–24
indicators.rationale: Household growth is the core of HUD market-analysis demand. Weak signal: only 35 of 394 tracts change by more than the ACS margin of error, so it carries weight 1. Changes inside the ACS margin of error are treated as zero change.

indicators.label: Home sales per 100 owner-occupied units, 2024–25
indicators.rationale: Arm's-length sales relative to the owner-occupied stock they come from. Dividing by all housing units measured homeownership share instead of market activity (round-1 review). Blank where a tract has fewer than 150 owner-occupied units.

indicators.label: Residential vacancy (USPS)
indicators.rationale: Low vacancy means existing homes are being absorbed. Blank for tracts with fewer than 200 residential addresses.

indicators.label: Job change, 2019 to 2023
indicators.rationale: Employment growth drives household formation (LEHD LODES). Blank where a block group had fewer than 250 jobs in 2019, since small bases give meaningless growth rates.

indicators.label: Rent growth, last 12 months (Zillow ZORI)
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0): 12-month ZIP rent change is lowest exactly where new supply lands, and it ran opposite to the rest of Demand (round-2 review).

indicators.label: New homes permitted within 800 m, 2019–26 (log units)
indicators.rationale: Revealed demand: builders are building nearby. Counts homes, not permits, on a log scale so one 224-unit building counts more than one house but doesn't swamp everything, and includes apartment buildings, which the City files as 'Commercial'. Unit counts are parsed from permit text (assumption where missing: 1). Several permits on one parcel (phases, trades) count once, at the largest unit count.

indicators.label: Market Value Analysis type (A strongest … J most distressed)
indicators.rationale: Default weight 0: rewarding strong markets steers housing away from distressed neighborhoods. Available for users who choose to weigh it.

indicators.label: Share of lot in the FEMA regulatory floodway
indicators.rationale: Used only as a gate: half or more of the lot in the floodway caps Site Feasibility at 5 and multiplies the overall score by 0.2; any part caps it at 40 and multiplies the overall by 0.6. Never averaged.

indicators.label: Share of lot in the 100-year floodplain
indicators.rationale: FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area; triggers the City floodplain overlay (Ch. 906).

indicators.label: Share of lot at 25%+ slope (City map, 2018)
indicators.rationale: Triggers the City steep-slope overlay (Ch. 906) and raises foundation cost. Half or more of the lot at 25%+ slope caps Site Feasibility at 50 (was three-quarters until 2026-09-27; any development in SS-O needs a Planning Commission hearing, §906.08.C.1). Not an overall multiplier: a hackathon SME described slope as added cost, not a deal-killer.

indicators.label: Share of lot in a City landslide-prone area
indicators.rationale: Triggers the City landslide-prone overlay (Ch. 906).

indicators.label: Share of lot on mapped landslide deposits (county: recent, old or red-bed)
indicators.rationale: County susceptibility mapping. 'Recent' alone covered 0.2% of parcels and none of the City's incident points; adding old and red-bed deposits covers half of them (round-1 review).

indicators.label: Share of lot over mapped mines (City undermined area)
indicators.rationale: Triggers the City undermined overlay (Ch. 906); subsidence risk. Half or more of the lot over mapped mines caps Site Feasibility at 70 and multiplies the overall score by 0.9: anything larger than a single house needs a mine investigation first (§906.05).

indicators.label: Known lead or galvanized service line at this address
indicators.rationale: Flag only (weight 0): the data has only lead/galvanized/unknown records, so it could only subtract, and it describes the existing house's line, not new construction.

indicators.label: FEMA NRI inland flooding score
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0). FEMA's National Risk Index score multiplies expected annual loss by a community risk factor built from social vulnerability, so it partly measures who lives there, not just the hazard (round-2 equity review). Parcel-level floodplain and surface-heat indicators carry these hazards instead.

indicators.label: Easiest legal pathway for mainstream housing types (current code)
indicators.rationale: Not averaged into Site Feasibility. It multiplies the overall score instead (see the legal block in this file).

indicators.label: Site availability (what is on the parcel now)
indicators.rationale: Not averaged; it multiplies the overall score (availability block). From the County assessor land use and class, owner category, the City vacancy flag, zoning (P, EMI) and overlap with mapped parks. First matching rule wins.

indicators.label: Lot area (for the sliver-lot check)
indicators.rationale: Not averaged. Lots under 600 sq ft (slivers) cap Site Feasibility at 30 and multiply the overall score by 0.3, unless they are condo units.

indicators.label: Low-income renters paying 30%+ of income on housing (CHAS)
indicators.rationale: HUD's 30% cost-burden standard for households at or below 80% AMI. More burdened renters = more need for homes they can afford. Left out in tracts where more than 30% of residents are enrolled in college, because student households read as low-income.

indicators.label: Renters at or below 30% of area median income (CHAS)
indicators.rationale: Extremely low-income renters are the households the private market serves least. Tract share of renter households; blank under 50 renter households. Student-heavy tracts can inflate it (not yet corrected). Left out in tracts where more than 30% of residents are enrolled in college, because student households read as low-income.

indicators.label: Median gross rent vs. rent affordable at 50% AMI (3-person household)
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0): rent relative to AMI measures how expensive the market is, not how many households are struggling (round-1 review). 1242.5 = 30% × $49,700 (HUD FY2026 Pittsburgh 50% AMI, 3 persons) ÷ 12.

indicators.label: Renters paying 30%+ of income on rent (ACS)
indicators.rationale: All renters, not just low-income; ACS margins of error are large at block group level. Left out in tracts where more than 30% of residents are enrolled in college, because student households read as low-income.

indicators.label: Housing + transportation cost share, median-income family (HUD LAI v3)
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0): modeled for a fixed household, barely varies within the City, and duplicates the transit and jobs access already in Access. CNT's H+T benchmark treats ≤45% of income as affordable.

indicators.label: Rent growth, last 5 years (Zillow ZORI)
indicators.rationale: Fast rent growth is a displacement pressure (Urban Displacement Project typology uses rent change).

indicators.label: Displacement Risk Ratio, 2019/20 (Reinvestment Fund)
indicators.rationale: Sale-price growth relative to residents' incomes (Reinvestment Fund). Data end 2019/20, so low weight; tract price growth carries the current signal.

indicators.label: Median home sale price change, 2020–21 to 2024–25
indicators.rationale: Median sale price change from pooled 2020–21 to pooled 2024–25 (county sales file). Blank unless both pools have at least 10 arm's-length sales.

indicators.label: Eviction filings per 100 renter households, 2025
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0): Eviction Lab publishes only ZIP-level filings for Allegheny County, and the ZIP value barely relates to the other displacement signals (r = −0.05).

indicators.label: Home energy burden, households at or below 80% AMI (DOE LEAD 2022)
indicators.rationale: Energy bills are part of housing cost. Modeled from ACS 2022 PUMS, not utility bills. Left out in tracts where more than 30% of residents are enrolled in college, because student households read as low-income.

indicators.label: Residents enrolled in college (ACS 2020–24)
indicators.rationale: Context and flag only. Over 30% triggers the student adjustment: the income-based need indicators are left out for the tract (a methodological choice). Includes dorm residents.

indicators.label: Weekday transit trips within 800 m, distance-weighted
indicators.rationale: Transit Score pattern: trips × mode weight × distance decay.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest supermarket
indicators.rationale: USDA SNAP-authorized supermarkets and super stores only. The broader 'full_grocery' tier included convenience/dollar stores and stale permit rows (round-1 review). Walk Score decay: full credit within 400 m, none beyond 2.4 km. Straight-line distance.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest small grocery store
indicators.rationale: SNAP 'Grocery Store' type: smaller grocers that carry staples.

indicators.label: Shops and restaurants within 800 m
indicators.rationale: A main-street proxy (WPRDC food-facility and business points). Raised agreement with Walk Score from 0.85 to 0.90 in the round-1 review.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest pharmacy
indicators.rationale: Retail pharmacies from the CMS NPPES registry (2026), with closed Rite Aid stores removed.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest school
indicators.rationale: Proximity only; school quality is deliberately not scored.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest park
indicators.rationale: Distance to the nearest park boundary. Tightened (full credit within 200 m, none beyond 1.2 km) because nearly every parcel was near some park.

indicators.label: Distance to nearest health center, clinic or hospital
indicators.rationale: HRSA health-center sites, NPPES urgent-care/primary-care/community clinics, and hospitals.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest child care
Walking distance to nearest library
Walking distance to nearest food pantry or walk-up food distribution
indicators.rationale: Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank network (Apr 2025). Drive-up distributions are excluded because they are scheduled events, not places you can walk to.

indicators.label: Distance to nearest dentist
indicators.rationale: OSM + County Assets. No data on which dentists accept Medicaid.

indicators.label: Walking distance to nearest community center
Distance to nearest senior center
indicators.rationale: Matters most for older adults; the older-adult preset raises Access overall.

indicators.label: Jobs reachable within 30 minutes by transit
indicators.rationale: Cumulative-opportunity accessibility (EPA Smart Location Database style).

indicators.label: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5), PA percentile
indicators.rationale: EJScreen v2.3 modeled annual exposure, re-ranked within the county.

indicators.label: Traffic combustion (mean of diesel PM, NO2 and traffic proximity percentiles)
indicators.rationale: Three correlated traffic indicators averaged first so traffic counts once.

indicators.label: Industrial air toxics (RSEI), PA percentile
Industrial PM2.5 emissions nearby, distance-weighted (ACHD, ≤2021)
indicators.rationale: PM2.5 tons/yr (filterable + condensable) from current permitted facilities, full weight within 1 km, fading to zero at 10 km so Clairton Coke Works reaches the Mon Valley neighborhoods. Excludes NRG Cheswick, which stopped generating on March 31, 2022. Emissions, not measured exposure; the inventory ends in 2021.

indicators.label: Modeled annual household VMT, median-income family (HUD LAI v3)
indicators.rationale: Transportation-carbon proxy. HUD models VMT for a fixed household (median income, 4 people, 2 commuters), so it varies only with location efficiency. Inputs 2012–16, 2010 tracts.

indicators.label: FEMA NRI heat wave score
indicators.rationale: Context only (weight 0). FEMA's National Risk Index score multiplies expected annual loss by a community risk factor built from social vulnerability, so it partly measures who lives there, not just the hazard (round-2 equity review). Parcel-level floodplain and surface-heat indicators carry these hazards instead.

indicators.label: Summer surface heat, parcel (Landsat 8, 4-scene anomaly vs county median)
indicators.rationale: Mean of (LST − scene county median) over 4 clear summer scenes, 2023–2025. Surface, not air, temperature; ranked, not thresholded.

indicators.label: Tree canopy around the parcel (block-group mean, NLCD 2021)
indicators.rationale: Block-group mean canopy. The single 30 m pixel at the parcel centroid read 0 for a quarter of parcels (round-1 review).

sensitivity.rationale: Dirichlet draws around the current pillar weights. Concentration 47 gives a 0.2 weight a standard deviation of about 0.058, matching the ±0.1 uniform weight ranges used in the JRC audit of the Global Innovation Index.

units.fraction_pct: value is a fraction; shown ×100 as %

verdict.about: Can this housing type be built here? A red / yellow / green verdict per typology, computed from pass/fail checks (zoning pathway, site hazards, site availability, lot size, physical fit), never from the weighted score. It answers a different question from the pillars: the pillars rank how good a place is; the verdict says what stands in the way. Framing suggested by a hackathon housing SME (2026-09-27): red = not developable, yellow = could be developable with variances or subsidy, green = developable as-is. Money is not checked: whether the project pencils is not assessed.

levels.yellow: Possible, with extra approvals or site cost
levels.green: No blockers found in our checks

verdict.not_checked: Not checked: whether it pencils (construction cost vs. value), soils, contamination, and utility lines. Decision support only, not legal, financial or zoning advice.

pathway_time.about: How long each approval can take before a building permit, shown with the pathway reason so hearings read as time and carrying cost, not just a probability (hackathon SME, 2026-09-27: variances are usually granted, but the time and expense make lots hard to develop). Code deadlines are maximums from the City code; the rezoning figure is observed.
pathway_time.za: decision due 21 days after a complete application (§922.08)
pathway_time.zbe_special_exception: hearing within 45 days, decision within 45 days after: up to about 3 months (§922.07)
pathway_time.conditional_use: up to about 6 months across Planning Commission and Council (§922.06)
pathway_time.not_permitted: a use variance runs on the ZBA clock (about 3 months); site rezonings took a median 123 days at Council (2015–26, 42 of 49 adopted)
pathway_time.permit_note: Then the building permit: median 120–200 days to issue for new residential, 2019–26 (WPRDC PLI permits).

side_setbacks.source: Pittsburgh Code §903.03 as amended Ord. 10-2025 (eff. 2025-05-07), read on eCode360 2026-09-26: research/sources/ecode360-2026-09-26-pittsburgh-903-03-dimensional-standards.md
side_setbacks.about: Total interior side setback (both sides, ft) by base district and density suffix. Buildable width = lot width minus this. Attached (party-wall) housing has no interior side setback, so it is skipped. Corner-lot exterior side setbacks and contextual setbacks (§925.06) are not modeled. Lot width is the short side of the lot's oriented bounding rectangle, so irregular lots are approximate.
side_setbacks.min_building_width_note: Assumption: about the narrowest practical detached building (a narrow Pittsburgh rowhouse is ~14–16 ft). Below this, a hackathon SME's example (24 ft RM-M lot, two 10 ft setbacks, 4 ft left) says a dimensional variance is likely granted but costs time and money.

legal.description: Whether current zoning lets you build the brief's mainstream housing types (detached, townhouse, two-unit, three-unit, multi-unit) on this parcel. The overall score is multiplied by the factor for the easiest legal pathway among them. Legality is read from the City use table (§911.02), not estimated.

levels.label: Housing allowed with Zoning Administrator approval
Housing needs a ZBA special exception
levels.note: ZBA approved 90% of special exceptions in 2023–26 (n=30), counting only posted decisions.

levels.label: Housing needs conditional use (Planning Commission + Council)
Housing not permitted, but the parcel touches a district that allows attached or multi-unit homes
levels.note: Exceptions happen at district edges: a use variance or a map amendment extending the neighboring district. Since 2015, Council adopted 42 of 49 site rezonings and defeated none (7 held, withdrawn, pending or expired). But few housing use variances are in districts that don't allow housing.

levels.label: Housing not permitted: needs a rezoning or use variance
levels.note: Not legally impossible, but the slowest, least certain path.

levels.label: Planned district: depends on the site's approved plan
Outside City zoning jurisdiction (Mount Oliver Borough)
Zoning district not in our use table: verify with the Zoning Administrator
Hillside (H) district: detached house only, with ZA approval and Site Plan Review

legal.rationale: The multipliers are value judgments about how much approval risk should cost. 'Not permitted' is penalized heavily (×0.2), and ×0.35 where the parcel touches a district that allows attached or multi-unit homes, because rezonings (42 of 49 site rezonings adopted since 2015) and use variances do happen at district edges, though few housing use variances are in districts that don't allow housing. Approval paths are softened (ZA 0.98, special exception 0.94, conditional use 0.92, planned 0.96) because the ZBA approved 90% of special exceptions (n=30, posted decisions only).

overall.text: Among the stronger places in the City to build new housing.
A good place to build, with some trade-offs.
A mixed case: real strengths and real drawbacks.
One of the harder places in the City to build new housing right now.

demand.text: Strong demand: people are buying, renting and building here.
Weak market signals right now (few sales, more empty homes). New homes here will likely need public or nonprofit support.

site.text: An easy lot to build on: no major physical hazards.
Mostly buildable, with minor site constraints.
Real site constraints (slope, landslide, undermining or flood) to work around.
Hard to build here: serious physical hazards.

afford.text: Very high need: many renters here are struggling with housing costs.
Clear need for homes people can afford.
Lower measured cost burden than most of the county. Subsidized housing and small samples can hide need.

affordability.text: Very high need: many renters here are struggling with housing costs.
Clear need for homes people can afford.
Lower measured cost burden than most of the county. Subsidized housing and small samples can hide need.

displacement.text: Prices flat or falling. That can mean stability, or disinvestment.
Prices are rising: watch for displacement.
Strong price pressure on current residents. Income-restricted homes and tenant protections matter most here.

access.text: Everything is close: transit, groceries, health care and services.
Some needs are walkable; others take a car or bus.
Car-dependent: daily needs are far away.

climate.text: Low driving and a healthy local environment.
Mostly good on carbon and environment.
Trade-offs between low driving and local air, heat or tree cover.
High driving emissions and a poor local environment.

carbon.text: Residents here would drive very little.

local_env.text: Cleaner air, cooler surfaces and more tree cover than most of the county.
Some air pollution, heat or missing tree cover.
Worse air, heat or tree cover than most of the county.

phrases_note: The overall phrase uses the parcel's City percentile rank at default weights; pillar and sub-score phrases use the 0–100 score.

availability.description: What is on the parcel now. Vacant land and surface parking are the easiest places to add housing; occupied buildings, institutions and large buildings are progressively less likely to be redeveloped; parks, cemeteries, rail and rights-of-way are not development sites. The overall score is multiplied by the factor below.

levels.label: Existing occupied building
levels.note: Building here means replacing or adding to what's there. Where displacement pressure is flagged, replacing occupied homes risks direct displacement.

levels.label: Large existing building (20+ apartments, office tower, hotel, shopping center)
levels.note: Unlikely to be redeveloped for new housing soon.

levels.label: Institution (university, school, hospital or care home, church, occupied government building)
levels.note: Institutional land is rarely released for housing; when it is, it goes through master plans (EMI districts) or surplus sales.

levels.label: Park, cemetery or public open land: not an available site
levels.note: Converting parkland needs court approval (PA Donated or Dedicated Property Act); cemeteries are effectively permanent.

levels.label: Active railroad: not an available site
Unit in an existing condominium building
levels.note: Scores describe the building's location. Building new housing here would mean redeveloping the whole building lot.

levels.label: Right-of-way or air rights: not an available site

availability.rationale: Round-2 citywide review: occupied student rentals, hospitals and the County Jail ranked among the City's best places to build. Tiers are value judgments about redevelopment likelihood; vacant land ×1, occupied ×0.9, large buildings ×0.7, institutions ×0.6.

evidence_types.observed: Measured or recorded (counts, permits, sales, surveys)
evidence_types.modeled: Estimated by a model (EPA EJScreen air, HUD LAI, DOE LEAD, FEMA NRI)
evidence_types.assumption: Our assumption where data is missing (e.g. unit counts parsed from permit text)
evidence_types.policy: Current law or code (zoning use table)

preset_notes.market_first: Ranks strong markets highest. Correlates negatively with minority share (round-2 equity review), so it steers new housing away from disinvested neighborhoods.
preset_notes.affordability_first: Ranks unmet housing need highest; favors neighborhoods where low-income renters are most burdened.

climate.text: Low driving, but worse local air, heat or tree cover than most of the county.
A healthy local environment, but a car-dependent location.
Worse local air, heat or tree cover than most of the county.

site.text: A sliver lot: too small to build on by itself (could be combined with a neighbor).
